My wife and I just finished a cruise from Luxor to Aswan chartering La Rose for us 2. This cruise was supposed to be the pinnacle of our 1,5 months trip throughout Africa. But as often happens, our expectations don’t correspond to reality and La Rose cruise turned out not only to be the biggest disappointment on this very trip, but one of the most disappointing experiences throughout more than 25 years of us traveling the world.
The food was awful. In the beginning it was nearly impossible to communicate with chef Ashraf, even though our guide was translating. No matter what we were trying to ask for or explain, he was cutting us short, saying: “I know, I know” and proudly pointing on his shirt where it was written “Chef” in big letters. We have a set of very simple recipes containing very common products that we asked to cook for us at various – and sometimes very simple – lodges and several boats around the world: in Africa, Asia, South America. Cooks there in their majority were simple local people, but everyone always managed to prepare these recipes of ours with a higher or lower level of success. Super-chef Ashraf was the first one, who managed to do everything completely the contrary and end-up with something not eatable and nearly cold on top of everything. Even the salads: we tried to convey to him simple information, that we don’t like onion and peppers in the salads. And, of course, we got 2 big bowls full of both raw onion and sliced peppers. Even if one wanted to spoil something on purpose, one couldn’t do it worse. We tried for lunch the next day again, now with our guide putting accent to chef to listen better and figured with absolute certainty that he can’t cook anything on order, even an egg. OK, we changed tactics and asked him to be making what he supposedly knows how to cook from Egyptian food. From now on we were getting only Egyptians treats. Some even tasted not bad. But majority was either completely burned or half-burned. Then everything was kind of greasy. Every time I tried to eat something I had to force it down, though normally I like to eat and we are not unfamiliar with Middle East food. In addition, even though I am not prone, I developed some kind of allergy: as soon as we started eating my nose was starting to run without stopping. At first, I thought it was because of low-quality Egyptian wine we had to drink because of absence of anything else (speaking wine), but last day I stopped drinking it, but allergy persisted. Finally, we figured to ask The Chef: what are you cooking on? – On corn oil, - the answer was. Needless to add: on low quality oil sold by bulk. If to look-up side effects of corn oil it is possible to discover stomach irritation, potential toxicity, increased risk of cardiovascular decease and weight gain. As soon as we were out of La Rose, the allergy stopped.
They also have another chef, obviously for the crew, I met him several times when being on upper deck. He was passing-by without even saying hello, like I didn’t exist. Interesting attitude towards clients.
Dahabiyas must be stationary during the night and for the first one the crew docked it so that it was constantly beaten against whatever it was docked against with loud bangs. Numerous times I told them to fix it and was assured that from now on we won’t be disturbed, but it kept banging the whole night, so we couldn’t sleep properly. And morning after we were passing a river-lock at Esna and the impact was as if the boat hit something hard at full speed. BANG!!! All doors opened, all fire-extinguishers fell from the wall. Just by pure luck my wife happened to be nearby and managed to catch all our photo- and video-equipment being on its way to the floor. “We shouldn’t worry, we were just passing a lock”, - we were told. Somehow my question: would you buy us new photo equipment, if ours got smashed by hitting the floor? – went unanswered.
Finally, as it turned the sites that we saw on the way, some of them were OK, but nothing special, we already saw much more interesting ones, when based in Luxor.
Once in a lifetime experience learning and discovering ancient Egyptian history and culture. The cruise is the best way to experience the beauty and magnificence of the Nile.

Our Dahabiya experience was truly unforgettable and one of the highlights of our trip to Egypt.

The boat itself was beautiful, elegant, and very well maintained, offering a peaceful and intimate way to explore the Nile. Sailing on a traditional Dahabiya rather than a large cruise ship made the experience feel much more authentic and relaxing.

The staff on board were incredibly kind, attentive, and always willing to help with a smile. They created a warm and welcoming atmosphere throughout the journey.

We also really appreciated the excursions, which were well organized and allowed us to visit stunning historical sites while avoiding the crowds of larger cruises. A special mention as well to our guide, who was very helpful and supportive during the trip.

What also stood out was the professionalism and care shown by the company in handling communication before, during, and after the trip. It showed a genuine commitment to customer satisfaction, which we greatly appreciated.

Overall, this was a unique and memorable way to discover the Nile, and we would definitely recommend this experience to anyone looking for a more personal and charming alternative to traditional cruises.

Before booking my trip I was a little unsure. Almost every Nile cruise promotes itself as a luxury cruise, so I wondered what the real standard of luxury in Egypt was. Would it truly be as promised, and would the price be worth it? I finally chose to follow the idea of affordable luxury, thinking that if it turned out to be less than expected, at least I would not regret the money too much.
When I finally experienced the Oberoi Zahra I realized it was worth every penny. In fact it offered far more than I expected.
The food was one of the highlights. Every meal was carefully prepared, beautifully presented and full of flavor. It felt like dining at the level of a three Michelin star chef. The service was just as impressive. From housekeeping to the manager, every member of the staff was attentive, thoughtful and always ready to help. Their genuine care and attention to detail made the journey unforgettable.
The facilities on board were excellent. There was a swimming pool, a gym, a spa, a rooftop bar and even private jacuzzis. With only a limited number of cabins, the atmosphere always felt calm and private, never crowded. That sense of space and exclusivity made the trip even more enjoyable.
The excursions along the way were equally remarkable. At every stop there were private guides who explained the history and culture. Transfers were handled directly by Oberoi, which made everything smooth and convenient. I never had to think about planning because every detail was taken care of.
For me, traveling with the Oberoi Zahra was not just a river cruise. It was a journey that combined comfort, elegance and a deep connection with Egypt’s ancient heritage. It is one of those rare experiences where you truly receive more than what you pay for, and it is a memory I will always treasure.

The owner is a lovely person and made us feel welcomed, food delicious and the portions are big! The views from the Terrasse are lovely! Thank you for a wonderful last night! 100% recommend!

This was the only place so far where we did not feel like tourists. From the moment we arrived, it was very welcoming and relaxed. Sunflower Nile Roof Restaurant is easy to get to on the West Bank in Luxor. We popped down from Jolie Ville and it sits directly opposite El Kababgy, making it a quick boat ride across the Nile. We visited at lunchtime and were the only people there, as it gets busy in the evening, which made the experience calm and unhurried.

The owner was genuinely kind, easy to talk to, and very hospitable. He promised excellent food and fully delivered. The drinks were great too. We had a fresh strawberry smoothie, mint in hot water for me, and a non alcoholic mojito, all refreshing and well prepared.

I am always looking for good clay pot cooking in any country, although here it is usually sold as tagine. We ordered several clay pot dishes along with mixed plates, and the food was outstanding. The flavours were spot on, with juicy chicken and fish, properly cooked potatoes, and rice with noodles done just right. There was everything you want in a meal, flavour, moisture, balance, and quality. I am usually the first to complain in most restaurants, but this food was too good to fault.

Prices were Egyptian, with no con and no surprises. Everything was clearly listed on the menu and totally transparent. All of us ate and drank for less than 1200 EGP, which made the experience even better.

The bread was the only thing that was not to my personal taste, as it leaned towards a healthier style. I prefer white Egyptian bread, but the rest of the family ate it all without hesitation. The salad was fresh and crisp, and the clay pot dishes really stood out for how well everything was cooked and seasoned. To finish, the owner treated us to some huge fresh strawberries, which was a very generous touch.

Everything was cooked, served, and eaten within an hour. The experience was excellent and we genuinely wished we could have stayed longer. That said, we are going back tomorrow evening, which says everything.

We stayed at this hotel for four days.
When we arrived at the hotel, we thought it was a strange location, right down an alley.
Inside there were more surprises like the reception being outside, and the “restaurant” actually being a VERY small bar. They do have a kitchen in the back.
The pool was great, and we swam there everyday which was refreshing after going to the valley of the kings in 38 degree weather.
We had an amazing view of the valley and it was beautiful when it lit up in the evening.
The rooms weren’t the best either.
There was a crack when we closed the door and a hole at the bottom so you can see through it.
The beds were very hard because you can feel the springs through the mattress and there’s a long metal stick that you can feel on the side.
I also got a stiff neck from the pillow the first day. But i got used to it and slept very good the other nights.
The doors are very hard to close.
You have to push them very hard to close it.
The front door of the room is very hard to open, which makes you think it’s still locked.
The shower was nice till the day last day.
It went from very cold to very hot, and kept either going hard or sprinkling down a few drops of water.
At first the service was very fast but it kept getting slower until it took a full half an hour for them to bring the drinks.
But needless to say, the people that work there are very nice!
They are always there if you need them and once they noticed what we didn’t like (like some things in the breakfast) they immediately improved it and left out the things we didn’t eat.
When you get to the hotel late like at nine in the evening, they lock the gate so there is a door bell on the side of the door next to it, but that doesn’t always work. We just ended up calling them every time since they don’t hear us knock I guess.
There is a mosque right next to the hotel so you’ll probably wake up at four a clock because of the call to prayer.
The drain by the shower was broken and was very sharp so for people who don’t have the best vision it might be a risk, since you can get cut.
It sounds like a very negative review but once you stay there a day or two, you’ll get used to it, and then it’s not so bad.

Panorama Hotel Luxor – a true home away from home
We stayed at the Panorama Hotel in Luxor as a family, and this choice truly made our trip special. Located on the West Bank, the hotel offers a calm, authentic setting that is perfect for families.
From the very first day, the level of care was exceptional. Despite our flight arriving late at around 1 a.m., Ayman personally came to pick us up, making our arrival completely stress-free after a long journey. This kind of attention perfectly reflects the spirit of the place.
The West Bank is, in our opinion, the best area to stay in Luxor. Unlike the East Bank, where you can hardly walk a few meters without being approached by taxis, horse carriages or motorboats, the West Bank allows you to relax, move around peacefully and experience the real rhythm of Egypt: villages, craftsmen, landscapes and everyday local life.
The hotel is ideally located near Luxor’s main archaeological sites: the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Nobles, Deir el-Bahari (Hatshepsut Temple) and the Ramesseum. This makes sightseeing easy and stress-free, especially when traveling with children.
Crossing the Nile to the East Bank is quick, easy and very affordable (just a few minutes by ferry for around 1 euro). From there, it is easy to reach the city center and even walk to Karnak Temple, while enjoying the peace and quiet of the West Bank in the evening.
We were given a spacious apartment with two bedrooms and a living room, which immediately made us feel at home. This truly reflects the spirit of a real guesthouse, ideal for families.
The hotel offers all the essential comforts, with good restaurants nearby and a relaxed atmosphere. And the view is simply spectacular — not a 180° view, but a stunning 360° panorama over the Nile, the temples, the Theban mountains and unforgettable sunsets.
Finally, the kindness and availability of our hosts, especially Ayman, made all the difference. From lending books about Luxor and Egypt to organizing transfers and even a hot-air balloon ride, everything was done to make our stay easy and memorable.
👉 Calm, authenticity, comfort and outstanding hospitality.
We already can’t wait to return and highly recommend the Panorama Hotel Luxor.

The Tomb of Ramses III is one of the most impressive and well-preserved tombs in the Valley of the Kings. It belongs to the great Pharaoh Ramses III, one of the last powerful rulers of the New Kingdom. The tomb is famous for its beautiful wall paintings that depict scenes from the Book of the Dead, Book of Gates, and Book of Amduat, showing the pharaoh’s journey to the afterlife. The vibrant colors and detailed carvings reflect the artistic excellence and religious beliefs of ancient Egypt.

The scene of the harpist inside the tomb of Ramses III is one of the most captivating depictions, reflecting the ancient Egyptians’ deep love for music and its sacred role in rituals and celebrations. The musician is shown gently playing the ancient Egyptian harp, creating an atmosphere of harmony and serenity. This scene is not only a display of artistic beauty but also a spiritual expression — showing how music was believed to bring peace to the soul and connect humans with the divine in the afterlife.

As a professional guide visiting Egypt’s remarkable monuments, I consider the Tomb of Seti I to be one of the most extraordinary experiences in the Valley of the Kings. Also known as KV17—or Belzoni’s Tomb—it stands out as the longest, deepest, and most elaborately decorated tomb in this royal necropolis

Seti I? He was the second pharaoh of Egypt’s 19th Dynasty, ruling approximately from c. 1294/1290 BC to 1279 BC. He is respected by historians as one of the greatest warrior‑kings of the New Kingdom—renowned for restoring order after the Amarna crisis, reinforcing border defenses, and engaging in successful campaigns in Syria and Canaan  ￼. His massive building projects—especially the Hypostyle Hall at Karnak and the Temple at Abydos—helped reassert Egypt’s cultural legacy  ￼. Seti I is also the father of the legendary Ramses II, who continued his architectural and political ambitions  ￼.

What to See Inside the Tomb

Upon entering KV17, you’ll be immersed in an artistic and spiritual labyrinth. The tomb follows a “joggled axis” plan, descending through chambers labeled A–D until reaching the pillared passageways (F, Fa, J, Jb, Jc, Jd), ending in a vaulted burial chamber with an astronomical ceiling  ￼.

The walls and ceilings are covered with deeply carved and vividly preserved scenes of funerary texts and rituals—featuring the Opening of the Mouth, Book of Gates, Book of the Dead, Amduat, Litany of Re, and Book of the Heavenly Cow  ￼. One highlight is a side chamber with unfinished stencil sketches, offering a rare glimpse into the ancient artists’ process: first rough outlines in red, detailed lines in black, and then color applied atop—an exceptional educational feature  ￼.

Exploring the tomb feels cinematic—descend staircases and wooden-slatted ramps, passing through candlelit corridors into a vast burial chamber where the art and atmosphere become truly immersive  ￼. It’s sometimes a solitary experience thanks to its price and exclusivity

This tomb is not included in the standard Valley of the Kings ticket. Entry requires a separate, special ticket, In September 2025, the entrance fee for the Tomb of Seti I is EGP 2000—a premium extra ticket beyond the main Valley of the Kings admission  ￼.

This makes it the most expensive tomb in the Valley—costing significantly more than three times the standard entry price for multiple tombs  ￼.

Tip: Plan to spend at least 45 minutes to 1 hour inside the tomb to fully appreciate its scale and artistry.

Bring comfortable shoes—the descent involves many stairs and ramps.

Morning or late-day visits can offer more solitude—quiet firsthand immersion often elevates the experience  ￼.

A Grand but Abandoned Tomb Later Reused as a Workshop and Storage Area

KV4 is one of the most unusual tombs in the valley. Intended for Ramesses XI, the last king of the New Kingdom, it was never completed or used for burial. Instead, it became a kind of “industrial space” during the Third Intermediate Period.

Archaeological evidence shows that KV4 was repurposed as:

A workshop for dismantling and rewrapping royal mummies

A storage area for funerary equipment

A processing site for materials removed from earlier tombs

The architecture is large and ambitious, with wide corridors and a spacious burial chamber — a reminder that Ramesses XI still envisioned a grand royal tomb despite the kingdom’s collapse.

KV4’s unfinished walls, tool marks, and later modifications make it a rare archaeological archive of tomb reuse, restoration practices, and the chaotic final years of the Valley of the Kings as an active necropolis.

The tomb of Merenptah, known to Egyptologists as KV8, is one of the largest and most impressive burial places in the Valley of the Kings at Luxor. Merenptah was the 13th son of Ramesses II and came to the throne late in life, ruling Egypt from around 1213 to 1203 BCE during the 19th Dynasty. His reign was marked by military campaigns against invading Libyans and the so-called “Sea Peoples,” victories that were later inscribed on the famous “Israel Stele.”

Because he inherited the throne at an advanced age, Merenptah had little time to prepare his eternal resting place, yet his tomb reflects both grandeur and architectural ambition. Stretching nearly 160 meters into the rock, KV8 is among the longest in the valley. The entrance corridor leads through a series of descending passageways and pillared chambers, decorated with religious texts such as the Book of Gates, the Book of Caverns, and the Amduat, all of which guided the king’s soul safely through the underworld. The reliefs and hieroglyphs still retain traces of their original colors, giving visitors a sense of the tomb’s once dazzling appearance.

The burial chamber is especially striking. It was originally designed to hold a massive granite sarcophagus, so large that parts of it remain within the chamber because they could not be removed. The sarcophagus itself was nested, consisting of several stone layers, a style inherited from Ramesses II’s architectural traditions. Fragments of the red granite outer sarcophagus still lie in the tomb, while the inner parts were eventually transported to museums, including the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Although plundered in antiquity, KV8 still reflects the majesty of royal burials in the New Kingdom. Today, stepping inside the tomb of Merenptah offers a powerful glimpse into the beliefs, artistry, and ambitions of a pharaoh who, despite his short reign, sought to affirm his place among the gods and his illustrious ancestors.

KV1, the tomb of Ramesses VII, is one of the smallest royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings — yet its artistic quality remains striking. Built during a period of political and economic decline, the tomb reflects the shrinking resources of the late 20th Dynasty, but also the enduring devotion to funerary tradition.

The layout is simple: a straight corridor descending into a single burial chamber. Despite its modest scale, the walls are decorated with scenes from the Book of Gates and Book of Caverns, rendered in bold outlines and deep blues and yellows typical of the late Ramesside style.

The burial chamber’s vaulted ceiling is particularly beautiful, featuring Nut arching across the sky, swallowing and rebirthing the sun — a cosmic cycle Ramesses VII hoped to join. KV1 is a quiet, atmospheric tomb that captures the final artistic breath of the New Kingdom.

The tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings is one of the most extraordinary archaeological discoveries of the 20th century. Discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter, the tomb (KV62) is remarkable because it was found almost completely intact, unlike most other royal tombs that had been looted in antiquity. Though relatively small compared to the grand tombs of pharaohs like Ramses II or Seti I, Tutankhamun’s burial chamber contained a dazzling array of treasures—over 5,000 artifacts, including golden shrines, jewelry, weapons, furniture, and the iconic golden death mask. These objects are now displayed in GEM.
The highlight of visiting Tutankhamun’s tomb today is the chance to see the mummy of the king himself, displayed in a climate-controlled glass case within the burial chamber. The walls are decorated with vivid scenes from the Book of the Dead, guiding Tutankhamun through the afterlife. Tutankhamun's  tomb became the most famous  due to its preservation and the global fascination it sparked.

The TT188 tomb is that of Parennefer, the Steward and Cupbearer of the King.

His tomb is located in the necropolis of El-Assasif.
It is one of the few tombs in the Theban Necropolis that was carved and decorated solely during the early years of the rule of Akhenaten.

The tomb is decorated with sculpted scenes, some of which were painted. The scenes were all badly damaged and the name of Parennefer was carefully removed. The Tomb of Siptah (KV 47) remains one of the more remote, often overlooked treasures in the Valley of the Kings—making it an especially rewarding stop for visitors seeking quiet reflection and rich historical detail.

Discovered in December 1905 by Edward R. Ayrton, KV 47 is situated toward the southern end of the East Valley, cut into a rocky ridge rather than the main cliff face. This unique positioning means it’s a bit out of the typical visitor flow, lending a sense of solitude ￼.

The tomb’s architecture unfolds through three gently sloping corridors, leading to a pillared chamber, further passageways, and finally an unfinished burial room housing a large granite sarcophagus. Work on the tomb ceased when the builders inadvertently breached a neighboring tomb (KV 32), leaving much of the lower section unfinished and unadorned

Though incomplete, the upper corridors of KV 47 are richly decorated. The entrance features depictions of Maat (goddess of truth) kneeling and a solar disk. Inside, well-preserved scenes from the Litany of Re, Book of the Dead, Amduat, along with striking dotted-star ceilings, can be admired in Corridors B and C—many remaining vivid and fresh in appearance.Lonely Planet also notes that after the ornate entrance, the tomb quickly transitions into undecorated areas—a telling sign of its unfinished state.

Visitors can access KV 47 with the general admission ticket to the Valley of the Kings—which allows entry to three tombs of your choice from a rotating selection. This ticket typically costs around 750 EGP (~€13)  ￼. As of early 2024, KV 47 is frequently part of the rotation of included tombs—making it accessible without paying extra fees ￼.

What makes KV 47 particularly appealing for many travelers is its tranquil atmosphere. Unlike the bustling tombs of Tutankhamun or Ramses VI, its relative obscurity means it’s typically less crowded and more peaceful, offering a personal and immersive experience ￼.

El-Tarif is a necropolis on the West Bank of the Nile, at the site of ancient Thebes. It is located in the northwestern outskirts of Luxor and southeast of the VOTK just to the southwest of the modern village of At-Tarif. It is the oldest of all of West Thebes' necropolises.

Consisting of a small mortuary temple, and the farthest north of the Tombs of the Nobles, it contains tombs of the late First Intermediate Period, Second Intermediate Period and early Middle Kingdom. Old Kingdom mastabas are possibly attributed to local rulers of the Fourth or Fifth Dynasty.

Eleventh Dynasty tombs of local rulers have also been noted in the form of a series of rock-cut tombs dated to 2061-2010 B.C.E, the largest of which are Intef I to Intef III, who were kings of this dynasty.

One of the Oldest and Deepest Tombs in the Valley — A Monument to a Powerful Queen

KV20 is one of the earliest tombs in the Valley of the Kings and one of the most architecturally unusual. It was originally built for Thutmose I, but later expanded and reused by his daughter, Hatshepsut, the great female pharaoh.

The tomb descends in a long, twisting spiral deep into the mountain — a dramatic, almost labyrinthine design unlike later Ramesside tombs. The depth and complexity reflect early experimentation in royal burial architecture.

Fragments of decoration show scenes of Hatshepsut before the gods, emphasizing her legitimacy and divine birth. Excavations revealed two sarcophagi: one for Thutmose I and one for Hatshepsut herself.

KV20 is a tomb of ambition, innovation, and royal identity — a subterranean monument to Egypt’s most successful female ruler.

The Theban Tomb TT39 belongs to the ancient Egyptian official of Puimra or Puyemre.

It is located in El-Khokha part of the Theban Necropolis.

Dating back to the reign of Thutmosis III it is deemed a New Kingdom tomb.

Puimra was the second Prophet of Amun and had two wives named Tanefert and Senseneb.

The tomb is a unique architectural marvel, deviating from typical T-shaped tombs by featuring a columned portico and a transverse hall leading to three intricately decorated chapels.

Each chapel, rich in symbolism, reflects distinct scenes from Puimre’s life, honouring his significance, his family, and the customs of his time.

The hallway leading to the three chapels depicts various scenes, including inspections of the Temple of Amun’s workshops and activities, such as carpentry, jewellery making, stone-vase crafting, and ploughing. It also illustrates attendants managing horses and chariots.

The Avenue of Sphinxes and the Avenue of the Rams are not two different roads; they are different names for the exact same 2.7 km ancient ceremonial road in Luxor, Egypt. Also known as the Rams Road, it connects the Luxor Temple to the Karnak Temple. The route gets its varied names from the two distinct types of statues that line its path, both representing power, protection, and the gods: Statues featuring the body of a lion and the head of a ram.Symbolism: The ram symbolizes Amun-Ra, the chief Theban deity of the air and sun.Location: These are primarily found at the northern end, leading directly into the Karnak Temple.

The Alley of the Sphinxes, located between Karnak Temple and Luxor Temple, is one of Egypt’s most awe-inspiring ancient monuments. This remarkable path, once used for religious processions, is lined with rows of sphinx statues, each with a lion’s body and a human head, symbolizing strength and divine protection.

As you walk down the avenue, you’re transported to a time when this grand route was bustling with priests, processions, and offerings, leading to the grand temples on either side. The restored sphinxes stand proudly, their detailed carvings and massive size leaving a lasting impression on visitors.

The atmosphere here is serene, and the historical significance is palpable. Especially stunning when lit up at night, the Alley of the Sphinxes creates a mystical vibe that enhances the experience of walking through ancient Egypt.

For anyone interested in the beauty of Egyptian art and architecture, this site offers a captivating glimpse into the past. It's an essential stop for anyone exploring Luxor, offering a deeper understanding of the spiritual and cultural heritage of ancient Egypt.

Sondos Papyrus is a well-known chain of specialty art galleries in Egypt that specializes in producing and selling traditional Egyptian papyrus art. Often included as a standard demonstration stop on organized guided tours, the shops offer visitors an educational look into the ancient art of paper making before opening up into a large showroom. The business operates several large outlets situated near major tourist hubs across the country with outlets in Giza (Main Branch), Giza, Luxor, Aswan, and Alexandria. Staff members show you the step-by-step process of how the inner pith of the Cyperus papyrus plant is sliced, soaked, woven, and hammered under heavy pressure to form durable sheets. They also teach visitors how to differentiate real papyrus from cheap street fakes made of banana leaves. A popular feature of the shop is on-the-spot personalization. Artists can paint your name in ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics inside a cartouche on any piece you buy. The galleries feature massive inventories of art, ranging from smaller souvenir pieces to huge, framed reproductions of historical temple reliefs. Common themes include the Final Judgment, the ancient Egyptian calendar, and depictions of pharaohs like Tutankhamun. Visitors are typically welcomed with complimentary local drinks, such as cold hibiscus tea, in a clean, air-conditioned environment.
While the demonstration is highly educational and the paper itself is authentic, the sales pitches are very aggressive. While the papyrus paper is genuine, much of the base artwork on the standard inventory consists of high-quality screen prints or stamps rather than unique freehand paintings. The initial list prices are notoriously inflated. Experienced buyers report successfully negotiating the final price down by 70% to 80% from the original quote.

The Mortuary Temple of Seti I, located in Abydos, is a remarkable and historically significant site in ancient Egypt. Known for its incredible architecture and stunning wall reliefs, this temple is dedicated to Seti I, one of Egypt’s most powerful pharaohs, and also honors the gods and the afterlife.

The temple features beautifully preserved reliefs that depict important events from Seti I’s reign, including scenes of divine offerings and royal rituals. One of the most fascinating aspects of the temple is the famous “Abydos King List,” a carved list of pharaohs that includes many rulers from Egypt's history.

The temple’s serene location, combined with its awe-inspiring artwork and grand architecture, makes it a must-visit for anyone interested in ancient Egyptian history and culture. It’s a peaceful and significant site that provides deep insight into Egypt’s royal and religious history. Highly recommended for history enthusiasts and those wanting to experience the true majesty of ancient Egyptian architecture!

The Ancient Luxor Quay is a remarkable historical site that transports you back in time to when Luxor was a bustling hub of trade and religious significance. Situated on the Nile River, this quay once served as a vital docking point for ancient Egyptian boats and vessels transporting goods, offering a unique glimpse into the daily life and commerce of the ancient civilization.

The atmosphere here is serene and steeped in history, with views of the river and surrounding monuments. Standing at the quay, you can imagine the many ships that once arrived, carrying everything from tribute to sacred offerings, making it a pivotal point in the religious and economic life of ancient Luxor. The nearby temples and monuments add to the grandeur of the setting, making it feel like a gateway to the past.

It’s a peaceful spot for reflection and a great way to connect with the ancient city in a quieter, more intimate setting compared to the larger temple complexes. Perfect for anyone interested in the practical and cultural history of Luxor, as well as the role the Nile played in the development of ancient Egypt.

Mut Temple, located in the Karnak complex, is a hidden gem that offers a peaceful and fascinating insight into ancient Egyptian worship. Dedicated to the goddess Mut, the temple is often overlooked by many visitors, but it holds immense

Mut was a daughter of the sun god like Sekhmet, Hathor, Bastet, Nekhbet and others — goddesses known as the “Eye of Re.” They were both benign and dangerous and could appear as gentle cats or fierce lionesses. Because they influenced the Nile floods and could both cause and cure disease, their cults were vital to Egypt.

Mut’s other role, which assumed greater importance from the reign of Amunhotep III on, was as consort of Amun and mother of Khonsu. She is usually portrayed as a woman wearing the Double Crown, signifying her task of protecting the office of kingship and the king himself. Mut’s primary cult center was at South Karnak, linked to the Amun Precinct by an avenue of rams. Covering over 20 acres, it contains three major temples. The Mut Temple itself is girdled by a horseshoe-shaped sacred lake (the Isheru), a type specific to Eye of Re goddesses. The earliest preserved structures date to Hatshepsut and Thutmosis III, but the Johns Hopkins University Mut Expedition discovered evidence of a Middle Kingdom temple under the later construction. Until Dynasty 25, the Mut Precinct consisted only of the Mut Temple and the sacred lake.

The depictions of Pharaoh Ramses II and his Great Royal Wife Queen Nefertari are among the most famous and historically significant artistic works of ancient Egypt. In traditional Egyptian art, royal women were typically depicted as much smaller figures next to the pharaoh to emphasize his supreme divine status.  In the massive standing statues of Ramses II found at the Karnak Temple Complex and Luxor Temple, Nefertari is carved as a smaller figure clinging to the king's leg standing between his feet. This positioning represents her supportive role as his queen consort, acting as a protector and partner while remaining secondary to the god-king.
The statue was usurped by Ramesses VI (1143-1136 BC) and later by Pinedjem a High Priest (1070- 1032).  The king wears the nemes headdress with the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt and his arms are crossed, holding crook and flail; symbols of kingship.
Another take is that the woman at his feet is not Nefretari, but Princess Bent’anta holding a flower and wears an Uraeus crown of rearing cobras. Her name Bent’anta (Bintanath, Bint-Anath, Bintanat) is Syrian, meaning Daughter of Anath, referring to the Canaanite goddess Anath. Her mother was Isetnofret, one of Ramesses’s most important wives.

The statue of Ramses II in front of the second pylon at Karnak Temple is one of the most impressive monuments in the great open courtyard of the Amun precinct. This colossal figure was set up during the reign of Ramses II in the 13th

Many Colossi of Ramesses II were erected in the territory of Ancient Egypt . The most famous are those framing the entrance to the larger of the two temples of Abu Simbel , the one exhibited for a long time on the Cairo station square and now transferred to the Grand Museum , as well as the reclining colossus of Memphis .

Ramses II had two large temples built at Abu Simbel , one for his worship as well as that of the Egyptian deities Amon , Ra and Ptah , the other for his wife Nefertari .

At the entrance to the great temple are four seated colossi of Ramses II , one of which is believed to have broken shortly after it was built.

Meritamun, daughter of Ramses II, was an ancient Egyptian queen and a Great Royal Wife, and the eldest daughter of Nefertari. You're in Luxor, a city steeped in ancient history and often called the "world's greatest open-air museum." Here are some of the incredible things you can see and do:
East Bank of the Nile:
* Karnak Temple: The largest religious structure ever built, a vast complex of temples, chapels, pylons, and obelisks dedicated primarily to the Theban Triad of Amun, Mut, and Khonsu. Allow at least 3 hours to explore this amazing site. Don't miss the Hypostyle Hall with its 134 massive columns.
* Luxor Temple: A beautiful temple located in the heart of the city, connected to Karnak Temple by the Avenue of Sphinxes. It was built by Amenhotep III and Ramses II and was dedicated to the Theban Triad. It's particularly stunning at night.
* Luxor Museum: Houses a well-curated collection of artifacts discovered in the Luxor area, offering a deeper understanding of the region's history.
* Mummification Museum: Provides insights into the ancient Egyptian process of mummification.
West Bank of the Nile (Theban Necropolis):
* Valley of the Kings: The final resting place of pharaohs from the 18th to the 20th dynasties, including the famous tomb of Tutankhamun (additional ticket required). Explore the elaborately decorated tombs.
* Valley of the Queens: The burial site for the wives and children of pharaohs. Some tombs are open to visitors and feature beautiful artwork. The tomb of Nefertari requires a special, expensive ticket.
* Hatshepsut Temple: A stunning mortuary temple built for Queen Hatshepsut, featuring a unique terraced design.
* Colossi of Memnon: Two massive stone statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III, standing as silent guardians of the Theban Necropolis.
* Medinet Habu: The impressive mortuary temple of Ramses III with well-preserved reliefs.
* The Ramesseum: The memorial temple of Ramses II, showcasing his power and influence.
* Deir el-Medina (Workers' Village): The well-preserved village of the artisans who built the royal tombs, offering a glimpse into their daily lives.
* Tombs of the Nobles: Burial sites of powerful courtiers and officials, with fascinating depictions of daily life.
Other Activities:
* Hot Air Balloon Ride: Experience breathtaking panoramic views of Luxor's temples and the Nile River at sunrise.
* Nile River Cruise: A relaxing way to see the sights along the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, often including stops at key historical sites.
* Avenue of Sphinxes: Walk or drive along the ancient path that once connected Luxor and Karnak Temples, lined with sphinx statues.
* Sound and Light Shows: Enjoy evening shows at Karnak and Luxor Temples that bring their history to life.

Mind-blowing—Karnak is hands down one of the most impressive ancient sites I've ever seen! This massive temple complex in Luxor feels like walking through a colossal open-air museum of Egyptian history, built and expanded over 2,000 years by pharaoh after pharaoh. The sheer scale is overwhelming: huge pylons, towering obelisks, intricate carvings everywhere, and ruins that stretch out forever.

The absolute highlight is the Great Hypostyle Hall—134 gigantic columns (some over 20 meters tall) covered in detailed hieroglyphs and reliefs. Walking between them feels otherworldly, like being dwarfed by a forest of stone giants. The play of light and shadows makes it even more dramatic, especially in the morning or late afternoon.

Start at the Avenue of Sphinxes leading in—rows of ram-headed sphinxes guide you toward the entrance, setting an epic tone right away.

There's also the sacred lake (great for photos with reflections of the ruins), scattered obelisks piercing the sky, and countless smaller chapels and courtyards to explore. It's easy to spend 2-3 hours wandering (or more if you're into every detail).

The site is well-maintained with paths and some signage, but a guide really helps unlock the stories behind the carvings—otherwise it's easy to miss the significance. It can get hot and crowded midday, so go early for cooler temps and better light. The sound and light show at night is an option if you want a different vibe.

Our first day was an exploration of Luxor Temples and Karnak. Our guide Mohamed Ali introduced us to this magnificent historical site: Karnak Temple.
Karnak Temple is located in Karnak, Luxor Governorate, on the east bank of the Nile River in southern Egypt.
It lies about 3 kilometers north of Luxor Temple and is connected to it by the famous Avenue of Sphinxes, a ceremonial road recently restored and reopened.
As he told us, it's the largest columned temple in the world: it was built by more than 30 different pharaohs. Its construction began 4,000 years ago.
To access the Karnak Temple, you must cross a kind of bridge flanked by ram-headed sphinxes (symbol of the god Amun).
Inside the Karnak Temple, there are three main temples:
The central and largest, a sanctuary dedicated to Amun-Ra (God of creation).
To the left, a sanctuary dedicated to Montu (God of war).
To the right, a sanctuary of Mut, represented by a vulture (Goddess of creation and wife of Amun).
The importance of Karnak was that it's a major religious center,a royal treasury, an administrative hub, also a political stage for royal ceremonies and served as a  center for priesthood power.

The Temple of Edfu is one of Egypt’s most impressive and best-preserved ancient monuments, making it a must-visit for travelers seeking authentic history and mythology.
Located on the west bank of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, the Temple of Edfu was built during the Ptolemaic Dynasty between 237 BCE and 57 BCE, taking nearly 180 years to complete. It is dedicated to Horus, the falcon-headed god, who symbolized divine kingship and protection. According to legend, Edfu was the site of the great battle between Horus and Seth, representing the eternal struggle between order and chaos—a story vividly carved into the temple’s walls.
What makes Edfu remarkable is its state of preservation. Unlike many other temples that suffered from erosion or destruction, Edfu remained buried under layers of sand and debris for centuries, which protected its reliefs and architecture. When uncovered in the 19th century, its towering pylons, colossal gateways, and intricate hieroglyphic inscriptions revealed a stunning example of Egyptian religious architecture. Visitors are greeted by two massive pylons adorned with scenes of pharaohs conquering enemies and worshipping gods, flanked by granite statues of Horus. Inside, the temple’s hypostyle halls, sanctuaries, and courtyards reflect the grandeur and precision of ancient Egyptian design.
Edfu offers a rare glimpse into the spiritual life of ancient Egypt. Its inscriptions provide detailed accounts of rituals, myths, and temple practices, making it not only a place of worship but also a historical archive. Walking through its sandstone corridors feels like stepping into a living chronicle of mythology, artistry, and devotion.

The Temple of Kom Ombo is very unique because it’s dedicated to two gods at the same time, which is quite rare in ancient Egypt:
•	Sobek, the crocodile god, associated with protection, fertility, and strength.
•	Horus the Elder, linked to the sky, kingship, and order.

Because of this, the temple is perfectly symmetrical—two entrances, two halls, two sanctuaries. Everything is duplicated, and walking through it feels very different from other temples.

One of the most interesting details is the presence of ancient medical reliefs, showing surgical instruments, which highlights how advanced Egyptian medicine was. There’s also a small museum with mummified crocodiles, which is fascinating and adds something very different to the visit.

The temple sits right next to the Nile, so the views are beautiful, especially at sunset, when the light completely changes the atmosphere and makes the place feel even more mystical.

Helpful tips for visitors:
•	It’s a relatively short visit (45 minutes to 1 hour is enough).
•	Easy to combine with other temples along the route.
•	Bring water and sun protection—there’s limited shade.
•	A guide really adds value, otherwise it’s easy to miss the meaning behind the double structure.

Overall, Kom Ombo is not the biggest temple, but it’s one of the most original and interesting. Different, symbolic, and absolutely worth stopping for.

The location right beside the river gives the entire site an amazing atmosphere, especially later in the day when the lighting makes the stone carvings stand out even more. Arriving by the Nile made the experience feel even more memorable.

What makes Kom Ombo especially fascinating is its unusual symmetrical design, since the temple was dedicated to two different gods. Learning about the history and symbolism behind the layout made exploring the temple even more interesting. The hieroglyphs and carvings throughout the complex are incredibly detailed, and some of the medical carvings were surprisingly advanced for something created thousands of years ago.

I also really enjoyed the connection to Sobek, the crocodile god, which gives the temple a different character compared to many other Egyptian sites. Overall, Kom Ombo was a beautiful and very interesting stop that’s absolutely worth visiting if you’re traveling between Aswan and Luxor.

One of the main reasons we chose Go Luxor was their responsiveness - we had reached out to multiple providers and some of them just seemed to ghost us - Mike was exceptional in his responsiveness - any question, and we would have an answer within a few hours.
The high level of service continued through our trip with Mike constantly being on top of what was supposed to be happening with us. Alaa, our guide in Cairo was excellent, and Mike guided us in Aswan and Luxor.
They provide a level of service - private tours and customized itineraries that are usually found at much higher price points. If you are planning a trip to Egypt, they should be on your shortlist.
P.S. One point I wanted to mention is that most tour operators will take you to factories (Papyrus, Alabaster carvings etc) because  of financial incentives - Go Luxor never pushed them hard and when we declined, there was zero pushback. That was noticed and greatly appreciated.

We (my husband, our two children, and I) just returned from a 4-night, 5-day Nile River cruise from Luxor to Aswan.

Let’s start with communication and booking: While the company’s website looks polished, it was unusable when I tried to make a reservation. I couldn’t even get past selecting an itinerary. I eventually booked through Booking.com, but the information there was extremely limited as well. The biggest gap was around whether guided tours of the temples and sites listed on the itinerary were included—nothing was clearly stated.

I emailed and called multiple times for clarification but never got a response. This is something they really need to improve. Transparent information about what’s included in the price—and what isn’t—should be clearly listed on the website and booking platforms.

Upon arrival, we were asked to hand over our passports—something I hadn’t been informed about beforehand. They returned them the next day, explaining it was a government requirement for transporting guests between cities. While I understand that, it’s definitely something that should be clearly communicated ahead of time. We were also offered a tour package once onboard that cost us an extra $980 USD—roughly $300 per adult and $165 per child. That fee covered guided visits to all the temples and historic sites. While the tours were excellent, we hadn’t budgeted for this significant extra cost. Given that sightseeing is the primary reason for taking a Nile cruise, this should have been made clear at the time of booking.

Most of the staff had limited English proficiency, which led to a number of misunderstandings. While we managed, it would have made a big difference to have at least one fluent English-speaking staff member overseeing guest communication.

Food and accommodation were included in the booking, but drinks—even water or soda with meals—were not. At check-in, we were asked to sign a form acknowledging this, and we were billed for all drinks at the end of the cruise.
The food itself was just okay. At first, I joked that I’d lose weight by the end of the trip due to the lack of appealing options. The meals did improve slightly as the week went on, but overall, the menu was repetitive. Lunch and dinner typically consisted of a salad bar, soup, bread, a chicken and beef dish, rice and potatoes, and a pasta dish. I would have loved to see more authentic Egyptian cuisine, and my kids sometimes found it hard to find anything they wanted to eat.

One serious concern: I witnessed a staff member preparing hamburgers and using the same gloves to handle raw meat and then touch fresh buns. I avoided anything from the cold bar and I was extra cautious with food hygiene.

The ship itself appeared relatively new and well maintained. We regularly saw staff cleaning and keeping public areas tidy. Surprisingly, we were upgraded to a family suite (I hadn’t requested it), but the room had a strong, unpleasant odor—likely from cigarette smoke seeping in from the upper decks. I had to burn incense constantly, and unfortunately, we couldn't open the windows because the ships often dock side-by-side. I actually would have preferred the original room I booked, as there didn’t seem to be any odor in that section of the ship.

The excursions were definitely the highlight. Our guide, Mahmoud, was knowledgeable and brought Egypt’s history to life at each site. These tours made the cruise worth it. They also tried to include a few onboard activities—there was a small pool (though I didn’t feel comfortable letting my kids swim in it), afternoon tea on some days, a salsa night, and a Nubian show on the last evening. These touches were appreciated, though not exceptional.

All in all, the cruise delivered on its most important promise: showing us Egypt’s iconic ancient sites along the Nile. However, the lack of transparency, surprise costs, communication challenges, and mediocre food made the experience more frustrating than it needed to be.

I've always wanted to do a Nile cruise.  The last time I was in Egypt was 45 years ago, as a student, and didn't have the money to do a Nile cruise.  My travel agent booked myself and a friend on the MS Mayfair.  The ship was nice and the room was clean.  Since this was my first visit back to Egypt in 45 years, I wanted a room with a veranda, to be able to enjoy sitting outside and watch the Nile go by.  However, when we checked in for our cruise, the management and our tour guide pulled us aside.  Apparently they didn't feel that we would like our veranda room, with only a queen sized bed and tried to get us to take a non-veranda room, which had two twin beds.  Of course there was no mention of any refund of the obvious price difference.  After 10 minutes, they said we should go look at the rooms and let them know which one we wanted.  They watched us as we walked down the hallway.  I went into the veranda room first, poked my head back out of the door, yelled that this room was fine and then went back in and locked the door.  We had no problem throughout the rest of the cruise, all the staff being pleasant.  Apparently, in Egypt, they're not too keen about two men sharing the same bed.  The same might even go for two women or an unmarried couple, but I don't know for sure.  As I looked at the other cruise ships on the Nile, there weren't that many which appeared to have veranda rooms.  I wanted a veranda to sit out on, I didn't care if we had to sleep in hammocks.  FYI: the cruise ships park each night in tandem to other ships, so those with verandas on the right side of the ship, looked right at the side of another ship at night, not the Nile and the opposite shore.  I heard a couple complain about the gas fumes.  The food selection was fine, but in Egypt they tend to cook all meat well done, so it can be a little dry.  The nice thing about the Executive suites is that the drinks (alcohol and soft) are included, free and they let you take your drinks down to meals, to the sun deck and to your room.  Overall, it was a nice cruise, but my travel agent should have been aware of the bed issue and found us a veranda room on another cruise ship which had twin beds.

Considering everything, I would rate this a 3 to 4-Star cruise overall.

It’s decent for a family adventure, but there’s plenty of room for improvement in facilities and especially food.

I have to say, this trip was one of the best experiences I’ve ever had. The boat provided delicious food and a pleasant stay, making the overall experience fantastic. The staff were incredibly friendly, especially the kitchen team, who prepared fresh meals every day.We booked excursions, visiting various temples and ancient sites, which made every day an adventure. Our guide, Redwan, was excellent—friendly, organised, and ensured everything ran smoothly. Hats off to the entire team!

However, there were a couple of downsides. The constant burnt diesel fumes from the boat’s engine, which ran 24/7, became unbearable at times, especially when docked in Aswan due to the number of boats around. Unfortunately, this triggered terrible breathing issues for me, leading to a persistent cough for two weeks. Our room was one of the worst in terms of diesel smell, and while the boat was half-empty, they didn’t offer to move us. That said, given that we paid only £200 for a seven-night all-inclusive stay, I can’t really complain—it honestly seemed too good to be true at first!

One word of advice: don’t fall for the persuasion tactics to buy a membership. The system seems questionable.

Despite these minor setbacks, this trip turned out to be one of the best experiences I’ve had in Egypt. Highly recommended, but be mindful of the fumes!

We were on a 7 night Luxor to Aswan return trip. We were in cabin 328 next to our adult son who had joined us to see the wonders of Egypt. Tipping is done at the end of the trip and is E£4 per person per day, plus E£15 per person for your guide. Both these were as stated in our Discover Egypt paperwork. Our guide was Addel. We also tipped £10 pp for the drivers during the trip. This was done at the beginning. He was such a superb chap with an almost British sense of humour. Additional tipping can always be done.
Having said Luxor, the Jaz Crown Prince’s berth point is about 15 km south of Luxor.  So there’s little point in going for a wander in the evening.
It is a surprise to learn that the trip is made up of seemingly hundreds of other rather smokey cruise ships  - there is a smokey pall over the river.
At first it doesn't feel all that relaxing due to the rushing around seeing the various sites - but things do settle down. It is quite wonderful to glide up the world's longest river.
The food was fine but eventually felt samey. I developed a bit of a temperature and so didn't eat all that much. Amazingly my wife and I both lost a bit of weight, despite being on full board.
There is NO kettle in the cabin (luckily we took one), Also nights can be a little noisy with a general thrum of the boat's engines or middle of the night manoeuvres as other boats line up with each other - their crews and engines could be quite loud.
We did the optional Abu Simbel trip which took us almost as far as Sudan. It was spectacular, as was the desert sunrise. I foolishly paid in US$ on my credit card so was annoyed to find a 4.55% conversion charge levied by the local tour company, Wings. My Halifax Clarity credit card is perfectly capable of giving me a good exchange rate without an unexplained charge being put on. TIP pay for trips by local currency. Another trip is to take some single US1$ notes as they are very useful for tipping. Indeed the locals will happily accept $, € and £ in notes.
Beware that certain Mediterranean guests are not good at the usual queuing etiquette at meals.
All in all this was a trip full of fantastic temples and tombs. Such great memories have been made.

Egypt is beautiful, but I strongly advise against booking with this agency. Here is why:
The Only Positive:
Our Luxor guide, Mr. Mohamed, was exceptional. Despite English not being our native language, he was professional, patient, and deeply proud of Egyptian history. He even helped us take excellent photos and ensured everything in Luxor was seamless.
The Serious Issues:
• Dishonest Communication: Before paying the deposit, they were quick to reply. Afterward, they became slow (24hr+ delay) and even rudely accused me of not paying. When I provided proof, they showed zero respect or apology.
• Overcharging: They charge an unreasonable 7% fee on deposits. Later, they tried to charge USD 25 for a 6-minute hotel transfer that costs USD 0.80 on Indrive. We had to argue to get the "included" transfer honored.
• Tourist Traps: In Cairo, the guide pushed us into overpriced souvenir/perfume shops with poor reputations, ignoring our preferences.
• Terrible Abu Simbel Tour: After an 8-hour round trip, we were given only 40 minutes to see the temples. The guide yelled at us for being 10 minutes late due to the long walk/restroom break. A total waste of time.
• Lack of Transparency: In Aswan, the guide took us for tea without mentioning costs, then demanded payment afterward. She also ignored our requests for food when we were starving just to finish her shift early.
• Inflexible & Lazy: On our final day in Cairo, the guide refused to help us find specific shops in the market, allowing only 20 mins of free time because he was hungry, even though the tour ended early at 3 PM. They also tried to overcharge (USD 5) for a simple mall drop-off.
Verdict: I love Egypt and will return, but never with Black Camel Tours. They focus on "nickel-and-diming" guests rather than providing service. Do yourself a favor and book elsewhere.

Overall experience
We booked Black Camel Tours through Klook mainly because there was about a 40% discount, and the first two days around Cairo were actually well arranged and smooth. That good start was the reason we trusted them with more tours later in the trip, including Aswan and Abu Simbel.​

Cairo and cruise dinner
In Cairo, they offered a Nile cruise dinner option at an extra cost of 50 USD per person. From checking online, this seemed to be marked up compared with booking directly (around 35–40 USD), but we accepted it because the agency appeared to be doing a decent job and we valued convenience over chasing the absolute lowest price.​

Aswan tours and upsell
Because the first two days went well, we agreed to book additional tours with them to Aswan. We were clearly told that the first day there would be a full-day tour, and the second day would be a full-day shared tour to Abu Simbel with a guide included, and we paid extra on that basis. Our intention was to have things run smoothly, not to bargain hard, so we accepted the higher prices as long as the service matched what was promised.​

What actually happened
On the first day in Aswan, the local guide told us immediately that it was only a half‑day tour plus lunch, and the tour ended after that, which was not what we had been sold. The second day was even more disappointing: we joined a shared tour to Abu Simbel expecting a guide, but when we arrived the driver simply gave us two hours of free time and said there was no guide for us at all. Abu Simbel was one of the most important sites of our entire trip and experiencing it without the guide we had paid for felt like a huge let‑down.​

Response from the company
Afterwards, we contacted Black Camel Tours to complain about the missing guide and the fact that what was delivered did not match what was sold. They apologised and offered only a 30 USD refund, which does not come close to covering the guide cost and the mark‑ups we had paid them across the different tours. When we asked for a more reasonable compensation, they simply refused and repeated that 30 USD was all they would offer, so we eventually had no choice but to accept it.​

Recommendation to other travellers
This experience completely changed our view of the company, and it felt like they were more interested in maximising profit through upselling and mark‑ups than in respecting what had been agreed and caring about our experience. For future travellers, especially those planning key sites like Abu Simbel, the recommendation is to be very cautious and consider other operators, because once you pay, it may be difficult to get what was originally promised.​

I lucked into a 24-hour layover in Egypt—a place I’ve always dreamed of visiting—when my airline canceled my return flight and forced me to reroute. 😜 But the real stroke of luck? Getting Mahmoud from Ramasside Travel as my guide! An expert Egyptologist, he was an encyclopedia of knowledge about everything from ancient Egyptian history to modern life in Cairo.

We started the day at the Cairo Museum, which housed the world’s greatest collection of Egyptian artifacts until the brand-new Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza recently took the title. Still, the Cairo Museum is absolutely breathtaking, filled with ancient statues, hieroglyph-covered sarcophagi, and the treasures of King Tutankhamen. Most of his burial treasures are here—including his famous golden mask and two stunning golden coffins—but no photos were allowed for these masterpieces.

Standing before these 5,000-year-old wonders, I was in complete awe. Their sheer size, precision, and endurance are beyond imagination. Seeing them in photos is one thing, but standing at their base, you truly feel the weight of history. The towering limestone blocks, some weighing 80 tons, rise in perfect alignment with the sky, a testament to ancient Egyptian engineering.

It’s mind-blowing to think about how they were built—millions of blocks carved, transported, and stacked with near-perfect precision. Even today, their alignment with the cardinal points and celestial bodies amazes modern engineers. These structures have stood for thousands of years, witnessing the rise and fall of empires, the march of armies, and the ever-changing world around them.

Of course, I couldn’t visit Giza without a camel ride, and this was an experience I’ll never forget. The son of the camel herd owner took me on a half-hour round trip into the desert, where I got a panoramic view of all nine pyramids. Riding slowly over the dunes, with nothing but sand, sky, and ancient monuments around me, I could easily imagine what it would be like to journey for months across the desert like the caravans of old. There was a peacefulness and rhythm to it, and for a brief moment, I felt transported back in time.

Beyond the incredible sights, what made this day truly special was Mahmoud’s expertise, storytelling, and easygoing personality. The entire time, I felt completely safe, and there was never a lull in our conversation—whether about ancient Egypt, modern Egypt, or life in general.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Five of stars all around! If you ever find yourself in Cairo—whether planned or unexpectedly—Mahmoud and Ramasside Travel are the way to go!

We don't recommend booking with Ramasside  We booked a private VIP tour with Ramasside due to limited time during an overnight cruise stop in Egypt. The services provided did not align with the tour as advertised or confirmed to us.

I’d like to share our experience to hopefully save you from what happened to us.

We booked a private tour (just my husband and I) months in advance. A few days before, I got an email saying too many people signed up, so we’d be switched to a small group tour instead of private. As a “make-up,” lunch was included—something already in our package. We paid $1,050 for a private tour, so this was unacceptable. After pushing back, we were reassured we’d still get our private tour.

The morning of, while walking to meet our guide, we got a text—no pyramids today. The itinerary was switched to visit the museum and pyramids the next day. Disappointed, but we adapted. When we got to the meeting spot, no one was there. Their description said, “your guide and manager will be waiting with a sign showing your name.” That didn’t happen. After asking around, we learned our guide was late. Then, after an hour, we were told he wasn’t coming and were handed off to a stranger. We had no idea if this person was even from Ramasside.

The driver didn’t speak English. There was no narration, no interaction—despite claims that drivers/guides explain everything. The car’s seatbelts were broken, and the traffic was pure chaos. The car was ancient, with 285,000 miles on it, and felt unsafe.

About an hour in, the car overheated—on the middle of a 5-lane freeway. We had no idea what was going on, and the driver couldn’t explain. My husband (a mechanic) ended up helping him. It was 104 degrees, no AC, no ventilation, one warm bottle of water. It was terrifying. We were stranded for almost 20 minutes in insane traffic. We then drove two more hours with no AC, inhaling polluted air. I’ve never experienced heat like that.

We finally met the guide at the museum. We thought we’d get in an air-conditioned car—but no, he was on foot. He walked us to the museum, and I nearly passed out. I felt dizzy, overheated, and sick. The guide had no idea about our tour details—when the lunch was, what time we needed to be back, or anything. After the museum (which also had no AC), we were picked up by the same driver, this time in a different car.

Lunch was at 4:30 p.m. We were starving. It was on a boat on the Nile, which was a cool setting—but the food was disappointing. Just pita, dip, salad, and pickled veggies. I should start by saying that, compared to the "classic" 11-day cultural tour offered by the agency, we requested some modifications to include other interesting destinations (now I say unmissable, such as Abu Simbel, Wadi El Hitan, Dendera, and Abydos). The organization was excellent: every scheduled visit was conducted with guides and drivers capable of handling any situation. However:
• Having planned to take our trip in the second half of March, we were not informed that the first few days (in Cairo) would coincide with Ramadan; in practice, all activities ended early, taking away precious time for activities. In this regard, it would have been enough to modify the program, starting with the upper Nile, or to propose different dates to avoid the frustration of wasting our time (traveling is expensive, so time is precious and must be used to its fullest extent).
• We had made it clear from the start that we were intensive travelers, explicitly asking for each day's program to be optimized so we could complete it at the right time, taking advantage of the entire day. Instead, partly due to Ramadan, especially in Cairo, we were returned to the hotel at 4 pm (or even earlier); It's a shame that the hotel (right across from the GEM entrance, separated from it by a very busy 4+4 lane ring road...) is 20 kilometers from the interesting areas of downtown Cairo, denying us the opportunity to even take a stroll (Egypt isn't just monuments and archaeological sites; it also needs to be discovered in its everyday life).
• For the reasons mentioned above, we had the distinct feeling that the Cairo guides put their needs before ours. So, for example, for the visit to El Moez Street and the Khan Khalil Bazaar (which would have deserved more time and could have started after the GEM visit, which ended before 4:00 PM), we were picked up from the hotel at 6:30 PM and then stuck in crazy traffic all evening. In fact, we saw practically nothing (and these are UNESCO World Heritage sites).
• The second part of the trip, the so-called Nile cruise, was much better, thanks in part to our amazing guide, Hussein Fawzi. He understood the type of trip we were looking for and delighted us with his enthusiasm and knowledge, even suggesting some excellent extra visits that the agency hadn't even mentioned (even though, as elsewhere, we would have had time).
• As for the cruise (but it's not the agency's fault), it's actually a simple logistical support (you sleep, have lunch, and travel along a short stretch of the river); the motorboat is excellent, but what happens is that dozens of motorboats operate along the same route, on the same days, and at the same times (due to flights to and from Egypt), resulting in thousands of tourists crowded together at every stop. The height of surrealism is reached in Edfu (an extraordinary place, by the way), with the queue outside the site starting at 4 a.m., a rush to visit, and a quick return because the motorboat leaves at 6 a.m.... In short, in hindsight, I would suggest anyone who wants to enjoy the extraordinary beauty of this country to ask the agency to organize a trip (perhaps without the much-vaunted but disappointing cruise) that avoids the mass schedule of motorboats and includes at least a minimal amount of contact with local people. Furthermore, from what we've seen with car transfers, Egypt is diligently developing infrastructure in these areas, so road connections are mostly fast and convenient.
In short, the agency offers well-organized trips but (at least in our opinion) too standardized; if you really want to visit Egypt (and not just go there to say you've been there), you should expect a local agency to tailor the trip to your expectations, having all the relevant information. We will certainly do this for our next trip to Egypt, which we are certainly not finished with.

28. 04. – 11. 05. 2024  we spent 15 nights at Shahhat House. This is a beautiful, spacious, clean, comfortable house with a large terrace, in a quiet area of the West bank, right in front of Medinet Habu Temple. The house has a lot of space and everything you need for a comfortable and quality stay. Hamdy, the owner of the house, communicated perfectly with us. Since he was not in Egypt at the time we arrived, his acquaintance, Mahmud, stood in for him. He came to the airport for us, stopped with us in the Village to buy food, water and an Egyptian SIM card. He handed over the keys to the house, and arranged for us to have another great, challenging tour of the sights of Dendera, Gebel el-Silsia, and up to the Nile Islands in Aswan, and many other wonderful sights, exactly according to my itineraries. The house has a kitchen with equipment that is more than sufficient for preparing meals. Two beautiful bathrooms, always hot water. Comfortable beds. It's quiet around. A short distance behind the house there is an equipped pharmacy and a shop with water. There are two restaurants within easy reach. We went to Model Village for shopping by tuk-tuk (50 EGP for two) or by taxi, an acceptable price can be negotiated. Bakeries, lots of grocery stores, you name it. People here are friendly, always willing to help. There are many sights within easy reach. You can easily get to Luxor by boat from the port under the Village. Careful, always agree on the price in advance (we paid 100 EGP for two both ways). We just caught very high temperatures of 38 - 41°C. The house has air conditioning and fans. You only need to turn on the air conditioning a moment before going to bed, the fans ran all night. It was enough. We didn't use the washing machine, but we did use the fridge. Defacto, on the second day you get to know the surroundings and on the third day you already feel at home. I recommend this beautiful accommodation for both short and long stays. Six people can comfortably fit here. You can relax on the beautiful large terrace at sunset over the Medinet Habu temple.
We thank Hamdy and Mahmud for the unforgettable  experiences. Petr + Iva Praga V.

Tip 1) Bringing a few sheets of detergent is incredibly useful for using the washing machine. Long-term travel often means a lot of clothes, but using the washing machine can cut your load in half! Hotels charge extra per item of laundry, but the washing machine at Temple House was free to use, which was nice! The weather was dry, so everything dried in one night.
Tip 2) There are low, decorative steps at the beginning and end of the stairs, which are barely visible. I was unconsciously going up and down the stairs and almost tripped on the low steps. Be careful, especially when carrying heavy luggage.
Tip 3) We were on the third floor, and there's no elevator, so we had to carry our suitcases up ourselves (the owner, if he's around, helped us). Each of our suitcases weighed nearly 25kg, which was a struggle. If you're only staying for one night, it might be difficult to carry your suitcases up and down, so I recommend booking a lower floor or staying multiple nights!
Tip 4) If you turn left from the first-floor entrance and head out onto the main street, there's a supermarket. The water is cheap (no frills), and the owner is friendly.
Tip 5) It was a shame that all the nearby restaurants were closed around 10pm, but there's a Chinese restaurant 5 minutes away on the main street that's reasonably priced and open late.

Even after returning, this was a truly memorable stay, and I had a truly comfortable stay! I'll definitely stay here again next time I go!! I highly recommend it!!!!!

Give you the reviews of the Guest House and Some General Tips in Luxor

--- The Guest House ---

1. The room is good for the price – air-conditioned, with a toilet and shower inside.

2. The staff at the guest house are super helpful and friendly. If you respect them, they will also be nice and helpful to you.

3. The house is old, but they clean it well every day, even the corners of the room. Nice!

4. No need to take a taxi to Luxor Temple – it’s just a 15-minute walk to the ticket office.
I recommend going there in the evening, as the street is extremely hot during the daytime.

--- General Tips ---

1. If you take a taxi arranged by the guest house or hotel, you’ll have to pay more. This is very common here.
Uber doesn’t work here, so install the InDrive app – it’s easy to use and offers good prices.

2. Tour prices: There aren’t big differences between agencies, but the real price is not always clear.
The Booking.com app offers good prices so far, or find a good guest house has many experiences.

3. Install the Google Translate app and download Arabic.
Even numbers are written in Arabic, so use the camera translator of the app to check the real price.

4. Two nights and three days are enough to see most of Luxor’s attractions.

- One day for the west bank of Luxor, with a balloon tour in the morning and Luxor Temple in the evening.

- Another day for Karnak Temple and the east bank of the river.

5. If you don’t live here and don’t know Arabic, you might end up paying more and feel like you’ve been cheated. You could get angry,
but if it’s not a lot of money, just let it go.
Don’t ruin your whole trip over a small amount.

6. Learn some greetings in Arabic and use it often. It's a good start and big step.

Finally, enjoy sun and respect the people here. God bless you.

Bazaar Andalos is a typical souvenir shop in Luxor, selling a mix of alabaster items, statues, and general tourist trinkets. If you’re looking for a keepsake from Egypt, you’ll find plenty of options here, from small scarab beetles to larger decorative pieces. The alabaster vases and figurines are nice, and they often demonstrate how they’re made, which is a good touch.

Like most souvenir shops in tourist areas, prices are marked high, so haggling is expected. If you don’t negotiate, you’ll definitely overpay. The staff are friendly but persistent, and they will try to upsell. If you’re not used to this, it can feel a bit pushy, but it’s part of the experience.

Quality varies—some pieces are genuinely handcrafted, while others look more mass-produced, so check carefully before buying. The shop is well-stocked, and it’s a convenient stop if you’re looking for last-minute gifts. Worth a visit if you’re in the area, but be prepared to bargain.

We’ve been to Egypt many times. We’ve traveled extensively across Arab countries and consider ourselves quite savvy travelers. And yet — I’ll admit it — they got us this time.

The modus operandi is always the same:
Even if you clearly tell your guide (yes, even on private tours) that you are not interested in shops, that you value peace and quiet, and that you’re happy to reward that with a generous tip — you’ll still be led to a shop, restaurant, or café. Why? Because the guide gets a commission from whatever you spend.

That’s exactly what happened here.

We were pressured, rushed, and skillfully steered into paying far more than the products were worth. Looking back, it was a textbook manipulation, executed with a smile.

Experiences like this sadly do not leave a good impression of Egypt, despite the country’s incredible history and culture.

If you go: enjoy the little show… and then walk away.

Tourist trap. You are likely introduced to this place by your cab driver. Pricing is exorbitantly high compared to normal Egyptian standards.

We were given the menu with a fixed price of 650 egp/set. Past reviews from just weeks prior showed other menus with prices ranging from 350 - 500 egp/set. So I suspect they “tailored” the experience depending on the customers or the season. Not very cool huh.

Food, however, tasted quite decent. Small portion though, esp for the price we paid. Service okay. You can definitely find better dining options in the area if you do even a bit of research beforehand.

In general, be aware of places with thousands of Google reviews in Egypt tourist spots. Sometimes it’s not because they are good but because they have managed to trap many gullible tourists or they buy reviews.

​If you are exhausting yourself trekking through the West Bank tombs, do yourself a massive favor and skip the generic tourist-trap lunch buffets that charge you 100EP for a small bottle of water. Head straight to the rooftop at Ali Baba instead.

​The view alone is worth the stairs—you’re basically dining with a direct line of sight to ancient history, looking out toward the Valley of the Kings and the Colossi of Memnon. But unlike a lot of places where you pay for the view and suffer through mediocre food, the kitchen here actually delivers.
​I ordered a traditional beef shwarma with chicken pizza, and it was rich, deeply flavorful, and incredibly comforting. The shwarma was melt-in-your-mouth tender, and the chicken pizza a masterpiece, the chips got me by suprise, it tasted exatcly like that of a "wimpy" franchise . It’s easily one of the best meals I've had in Egypt so far and I started my journey from Cairo to sham El sheikh down to Luxor.

​The staff is lightning-fast, the presentation is surprisingly elegant for a casual spot, the toilets are actually clean, and they seamlessly accept card payments. Absolute gem of a lunch spot!

Pro-Tip: dont get sucked into the tourist trap restaurant with over charged meals, go to Ali BaBa and definitely have a fresh juice!
